title: On friendship
hookLine: a friend is a person with whom I may be sincere (Friendship, 1841)

cards: Scroll the contacts on a phone. Plenty of names. A coworker.
The plumber. Someone from a wedding. Old classmates who might not recognize your voice anymore.
Now a harder question: which of these names could hear a true thing from you, the unpolished version you haven't tidied up yet? Emerson asked something like that in his essay Friendship.
You met one line of it back on day eight hundred sixty-one. Today, his test for a friend, short enough to fit on a sticky note.

teach.h: A PERSON WITH WHOM I MAY BE SINCERE.
teach.b: First, the test. Emerson writes: "A friend is a person with whom I may be sincere. Before him I may think aloud." Not a finished speech.
The half-formed thought, the doubt, the thing you're not sure you believe yet. With most people we edit before we speak. With a friend, the editing can stop.
Second, what a friendship is made of.

In the same essay he names two elements: truth and tenderness. Truth alone can turn into someone who lists every flaw and calls it honesty. Tenderness alone can turn into someone who only says what you want to hear.
A friend, in Emerson's picture, holds both at once.

teach.h: THE ONLY WAY TO HAVE A FRIEND.
teach.b: Third, the way in, the line you've met before: "The only way to have a friend is to be one." So the test runs both ways.
Who can I be sincere with? And who can be sincere with me, because I've shown I can hear it without punishing them for it?

teach.h: BEFORE HIM I MAY THINK ALOUD.
teach.b: Fourth, what sincere is not. It isn't blurting, or honesty used as a weapon.

It's a friendship where the masks can come off because it's safe to take them off, a safety built slowly, by small true things said gently and received well. Even one friend like that is a great deal.

how: Readers of Emerson's Friendship often hold onto its two elements, truth and tenderness, as a way of judging and deepening their closest friendships.

o: Emerson's essay: a friend is someone you can be sincere with
a warning that true friends must always agree with you
advice to keep many friends so no one can let you down

s: Emerson says a true friend is one who always agrees with you

both together; either alone falls short.

games.q: a close friend asks how you're really doing. it's been a hard week and you haven't told anyone. what does Emerson's test point toward?
o: the true answer, said plainly and kindly.
turn the question back to them.
games.why: Emerson: "a friend is a person with whom I may be sincere. before him I may think aloud." a friend is exactly where the polished answer can be set down.

practice: Let one friend's face come to mind, and turn Emerson's test around: can this person think aloud in front of you? Remember the last time they told you something unpolished, and how you took it.
Then choose one way to make it safer next time: a question with room after it, a pause before advice, or a half-formed thought of your own, offered first.

wordCard.voice: On friendship. Emerson's essay, with its plain test: a friend is a person with whom I may be sincere, made of truth and tenderness together. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: sincere. Truth and tenderness, held at once by the same good friend. Until tomorrow.
